paragraphs: The paper studies federated classification when the available data are imbalanced. It focuses on maximizing AUC, an objective the authors identify as useful for this problem. Their starting point is that existing federated approaches based on directly solving a minimax problem have not delivered satisfactory performance. This motivates changing the optimization formulation itself.

The proposed formulation is a multi-level compositional minimax problem. In plain language, it combines nested stages of computation with an optimization structure involving opposing minimization and maximization objectives. The contribution therefore includes both a new way to express the learning problem and a federated stochastic algorithm designed to solve that formulation.

The authors provide rigorous theoretical guarantees for their algorithm and report extensive empirical evaluations supporting its effectiveness. These are complementary contributions: the analysis supports the proposed optimization procedure, while the experiments support its usefulness for learning. The paper positions multi-level compositional minimax optimization as a promising route for improving federated AUC maximization, and describes its study of multi-level minimax optimization as a first to the authors’ knowledge.
icml-2024-a-federated-stochastic-multi-l.tldr: The paper introduces a federated multi-level compositional minimax algorithm for AUC maximization, supported by theoretical guarantees and empirical evaluations.

paragraphs: Prompt tuning adapts a pretrained vision-language model by learning prompts that guide its behavior. The paper examines why this efficient adaptation can fail when test images differ substantially from training images. Its diagnosis is that text representations can become aligned with misleading visual features introduced by biased training data, rather than features that remain useful across domains.

CoOPood separates the alignment process into two contrastive phases, implemented through two lightweight projection layers. One phase brings text representations closer to invariant image features. The other pushes them away from spurious image features. This distinction matters because attracting useful features and rejecting misleading ones become explicit, separate training objectives.

The authors present CoOPood as a general framework that can be incorporated into existing prompt-tuning methods for vision-language models. Experiments on several out-of-distribution datasets show better performance than the state-of-the-art methods evaluated. The findings support the paper’s central argument: adaptation can benefit from controlling which visual information aligns with language, particularly when training correlations do not carry over to the target domain.
icml-2024-amend-to-alignment-decoupled-p.tldr: CoOPood improves out-of-distribution prompt tuning by separately aligning text with invariant visual features and distancing it from spurious ones.

paragraphs: A generative model can produce good-looking, varied samples without making it clear what is novel relative to a reference collection. This paper makes that comparison more specific: which types of samples occur more frequently in the generated distribution than in the reference distribution? Novelty here concerns the relative presence of different modes, or groups of similar samples.

The authors introduce a spectral approach to this differential clustering problem and propose the Kernel-based Entropic Novelty score, abbreviated KEN. The framework connects a numerical novelty assessment with identifying the sample groups responsible for the difference. That makes the comparison more interpretable than a score that does not indicate what kinds of outputs distinguish the two distributions.

The theoretical analysis considers mixture distributions whose components are well separated. The paper also develops a kernel-based procedure for estimating KEN from samples. Numerical studies using synthetic data and real image datasets indicate that the framework can detect novel modes and compare generative models. These findings concern novelty relative to a chosen reference, rather than an absolute judgment of originality.
icml-2024-an-interpretable-evaluation-of.tldr: KEN measures a generative model’s novelty relative to a reference by identifying sample types that the model produces more frequently.

paragraphs: The Segment Anything Model can identify image regions, but targeting a particular object normally requires a user prompt such as a point or bounding box. It can also struggle when downstream images differ from its general-domain pretraining data. Fine-tuning offers a way to adapt it, but limited training data can make overfitting a substantial problem.

BLO-SAM addresses these issues by learning a prompt embedding alongside model adaptation. The learned embedding enables automatic segmentation without manual prompts. Its bi-level optimization scheme trains the model weights and prompt embedding on different subsets of the training data, with each assigned to a different optimization level. This separates their training roles and reduces the risk of overfitting.

The authors evaluate the method on semantic segmentation tasks from both general and medical domains, reporting stronger performance than various state-of-the-art segmentation methods. The contribution joins two practical goals: automating the targeting that prompts normally provide and adapting a large pretrained model with limited data. The reported reduction in overfitting is a benefit of the proposed training arrangement, rather than a claim that overfitting becomes impossible.
icml-2024-blo-sam-bi-level-optimization-.tldr: BLO-SAM learns automatic prompts and uses bi-level fine-tuning on separate data subsets to reduce overfitting in semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a language model on a specialized text collection can teach useful knowledge while also teaching incidental patterns, such as an unusually strong emphasis on particular topics. The paper asks whether these two effects can be separated. Its proposed modification, conditional fine-tuning, performs ordinary causal language modeling with an additional context on which predictions are conditioned.

The central idea is that context can account for some statistical patterns in the corpus. When those patterns are explained by the context, the model can avoid learning them as part of the knowledge it acquires from fine-tuning. This gives the training process a way to be selective: retain information useful for downstream tasks while avoiding certain unhelpful corpus biases.

The authors report that this selective learning reduces forgetting and improves the tradeoff between retaining existing capabilities and adapting to new material. This matters because domain adaptation involves both goals at once. They also suggest possible benefits for lifelong language learning, where adaptation continues over time. That broader application is presented as a potential benefit, while reduced forgetting and the improved adaptation tradeoff are the stated findings.
icml-2024-conditional-language-learning-.tldr: Conditional fine-tuning uses context to explain away unwanted corpus patterns, helping language models learn selectively with less forgetting.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning language models on specialized data creates two linked challenges. Backpropagation can require substantial memory, while models can memorize sensitive information from their training examples. Zeroth-order optimization addresses the memory side by relying on forward passes. However, the authors explain that directly combining this approach with standard differentially private gradient descent becomes less effective as the model grows.

DPZero is a private zeroth-order algorithm designed to address that scaling problem. Its central theoretical result is a set of nearly dimension-independent rates. This means the reported rates largely avoid the unfavorable dependence on model dimensionality that motivates the work. The qualifier matters: the claim is nearly independent of dimension, not that every cost of fine-tuning is independent of model size.

The paper demonstrates the algorithm’s memory efficiency by privately fine-tuning RoBERTa and OPT on several downstream tasks. Its contribution is to bring privacy and memory-efficient optimization into the same training method, rather than addressing either concern alone. The theoretical result supports its treatment of dimensionality, and the experiments demonstrate memory-efficient private adaptation in the evaluated language models.
icml-2024-dpzero-private-fine-tuning-of-.tldr: DPZero combines private fine-tuning with forward-pass-only optimization and achieves nearly dimension-independent theoretical rates.

paragraphs: Federated multimodal learning must accommodate clients with different types of data and limited computing resources. Large models make this difficult because storing and adapting them can exceed client capacity. M²FedSA addresses the problem through a combination of model partitioning, lightweight adaptation, and knowledge transfer between clients with different available modalities.

The framework uses split learning to divide large models into modules, retaining only privacy-sensitive modules on clients to reduce local storage demands. It freezes the large models and introduces two specialized lightweight adapters. These support task-specific learning and modality-specific knowledge, allowing adaptation without training the full large model. The design therefore addresses where model components reside as well as which components learn.

M²FedSA also transfers multimodal knowledge to clients that have only one modality, operating at both feature and decision levels. This allows those clients to benefit from complementary information represented by multiple modalities. Experiments on several multimodal classification tasks support the framework’s effectiveness. The overall contribution is a coordinated approach to reducing client resource demands while maintaining useful adaptation across heterogeneous data sources.
icml-2024-enhancing-storage-and-computat.tldr: M²FedSA combines split learning, lightweight adapters, and multimodal knowledge transfer to make large-model federated learning more resource efficient.

paragraphs: The paper studies how learning features across several tasks can help with a new task when data sources have different input distributions and observations within a source may be statistically dependent. These conditions matter because they depart from assumptions used in existing theoretical studies of representation learning.

The setup assumes that all tasks share a nonlinear representation, with each task applying its own linear function to those shared features. The method first estimates the representation using N observations from each of T source tasks. It then fits a linear function for the target task using N′ target observations transformed by the learned representation.

The statistical guarantee separates target prediction error above the optimum into two contributions. Up to logarithmic factors, one scales with representation complexity divided by NT; the other scales with the dimension of the linear function class divided by N′. This describes how source data support learning shared features, while target data support fitting the task-specific function.

The authors report rates matching the independent, identically distributed setting, while requiring fewer samples per task than prior analysis and having no dependence on mixing time. Numerical imitation-learning experiments involving nonlinear dynamical systems support the analysis.
icml-2024-guarantees-for-nonlinear-repre.tldr: The paper establishes guarantees for shared nonlinear representation learning across differing input distributions and possibly dependent observations, with rates matching the independent-data setting.

paragraphs: A language model can make a false statement even when it can recognize that same statement as false in a separate evaluation. This paper investigates that discrepancy to show that hallucinations are not always explained by missing knowledge. It focuses on answers where an initial mistake is followed by an explanation containing additional incorrect claims.

The authors construct three question-answering datasets that elicit this pattern. When the incorrect explanatory claims are assessed separately, GPT-3.5 recognizes 67% as incorrect, GPT-4 recognizes 87%, and LLaMA2-70B-chat recognizes 94%. These percentages describe recognition of the incorrect claims studied, rather than overall factual accuracy. They show a gap between what a model says within an answer and what it can reject when asked separately.

The phenomenon persists with higher-temperature sampling, beam search, and zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting. The findings support a snowballing account: an early wrong answer can lead to further errors that the model otherwise might not make. This makes the sequence of generated claims relevant to understanding hallucination, alongside the model’s ability to recognize individual facts.
icml-2024-how-language-model-hallucinati.tldr: Language models can compound an initial wrong answer with false claims they can recognize as incorrect when evaluated separately.

paragraphs: Adversarial training teaches a classifier using images deliberately perturbed to mislead it. The perturbations are limited by a budget that is ordinarily applied uniformly across pixels. This paper reports that pixels do not contribute equally to accuracy on ordinary images or to robustness on adversarial images. That observation motivates changing how the perturbation budget is distributed.

Pixel-reweighted Adversarial Training, or PART, uses class activation mapping to identify image regions important to the model’s output. It preserves the perturbation budget in those regions and lowers it elsewhere when creating adversarial training examples. The resulting examples place more of the adversarial pressure on influential regions while reducing it in less influential parts of the image.

On CIFAR-10, SVHN, and TinyImagenet-200, PART improves ordinary-image accuracy without compromising the reported robustness. The result supports treating image regions differently when constructing adversarial training data. Its practical significance is an improved accuracy–robustness tradeoff in the evaluated settings: the method changes the training examples so that robustness training places greater emphasis on regions that affect predictions.
icml-2024-improving-accuracy-robustness-.tldr: PART reduces adversarial perturbation budgets in less influential image regions, improving clean accuracy without reducing robustness on three evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: Few-shot prompting adapts a language model by showing it a small collection of correct input-output examples. LEAP asks whether those same examples can provide more guidance if the model also examines mistakes it makes on them. The method converts errors into explicit task-specific principles that can accompany the original examples in later prompts.

The procedure first deliberately induces mistakes on the available examples. It then reflects on those mistakes to extract principles intended to help solve similar questions and avoid recurring errors. Finally, unseen questions are answered using both the original examples and the derived principles. This changes how the supplied examples are used without requiring additional examples or input from the user.

Evaluations cover multi-hop and textual question answering, reasoning, and mathematics. LEAP improves the tested models across the reported benchmarks, including GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4-turbo, and Claude-2.1. For GPT-4, the authors report improvements of 7.5% on DROP and 3.3% on HotpotQA over standard few-shot prompting. The findings support extracting reusable guidance from mistakes as a way to get more value from a fixed example set.
icml-2024-in-context-principle-learning-.tldr: LEAP turns mistakes on existing few-shot examples into task-specific principles that improve subsequent answers without requiring additional examples.

paragraphs: Searching from a reference image can involve intentions that visual similarity alone cannot express. Someone may want an image related to the reference through a semantic relationship, such as an inside view. MagicLens supports searches that combine a query image with an open-ended text instruction, expanding the range of relationships a retrieval model can handle.

The training approach uses image pairs found on the same web pages. The authors argue that these pairs contain diverse implicit relationships, which foundation models can turn into explicit instructions. This produces 36.7 million training triplets consisting of a query image, an instruction, and a target image. The web-derived relationships supply supervision for the retrieval task.

Across eight image-retrieval benchmarks, MagicLens matches or exceeds the prior best results while using a significantly smaller model. Human analyses on an unseen collection of 1.4 million images further demonstrate varied supported search intentions. Together, these findings support the central idea that instruction-guided retrieval can capture rich relationships beyond visual resemblance, and that naturally co-occurring web images can help train that capability.
icml-2024-magiclens-self-supervised-imag.tldr: MagicLens learns from web image pairs and synthesized instructions to retrieve images through diverse relationships beyond visual similarity.

paragraphs: Answering questions about first-person video requires recognizing small objects, filtering distracting visual information, and reasoning across space and time. The paper introduces Multi-Factor Adaptive vision Selection, or MFAS, to address these demands together. Its organizing idea is to select and combine visual evidence in ways that support the question being asked.

MFAS contains three complementary components. A patch partition and merging module supports recognition of small objects. A prior-guided patch selection module suppresses noise and focuses analysis on relevant image regions. A hierarchical aggregation network then combines visual meaning under guidance from the question. These components address the handling of local detail, the selection of evidence, and the integration of that evidence.

Experiments on several public egocentric video datasets support the framework’s effectiveness and generalization. The significance of the approach lies in coordinating these operations: preserving useful small-scale information is paired with selecting what deserves attention and assembling it into question-relevant evidence. The reported results support this combined framework for first-person video question answering, where recognizing an object alone may not resolve the question.
icml-2024-multi-factor-adaptive-vision-s.tldr: MFAS combines small-object processing, selective visual attention, and question-guided aggregation to improve egocentric video question answering.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations fit a signal using a neural network, but that fitting process can be costly. This paper treats training as a teaching problem: which pieces of the signal should the learner see at each step? Its Implicit Neural Teaching framework uses the signal itself as the target function and selects fragments for iterative training.

The target need not have a closed-form mathematical expression; an image defined by a grid of pixels is one example. The theoretical contribution connects two views of learning: changing an overparameterized multilayer perceptron’s parameters through gradient descent, and changing a function through functional gradient descent. The authors show consistency between teaching the overparameterized network and teaching a nonparametric learner.

That connection makes existing nonparametric teaching algorithms available as tools for selecting training examples during implicit representation learning. The reported experiments show training-time savings above 30% across several input modalities. The result supports example selection as a practical route to faster signal fitting, while the theoretical justification specifically concerns the overparameterized multilayer-perceptron setting studied in the paper.
icml-2024-nonparametric-teaching-of-impl.tldr: Implicit Neural Teaching selects signal fragments to accelerate neural representation fitting, with theoretical support and reported training-time savings above 30%.

paragraphs: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning considers uncertainty and potentially adverse outcomes when choosing actions. This paper studies that goal using an entropic risk measure and only a previously collected dataset. The offline restriction is central: the learner must derive a near-optimal policy from existing observations, rather than gathering new experience through ongoing interaction.

The analysis works within linear Markov decision processes. The first proposed algorithm is a risk-sensitive form of pessimistic value iteration, supported by a tight analysis that uses the structure of the risk-sensitive performance measure. Pessimism provides the organizing principle for learning cautiously from the available data while retaining the chosen sensitivity to risk.

A second algorithm incorporates variance information and reference-advantage decomposition to strengthen the guarantees. It improves the bounds’ dependence on both the space dimension and the risk-sensitivity factor. The authors describe these as the first provably efficient algorithms for risk-sensitive offline reinforcement learning, to their knowledge. The contribution is therefore theoretical and conditional on the stated linear setting: it establishes sample-efficient learning procedures for a risk-aware objective using pre-collected data.
icml-2024-pessimism-meets-risk-risk-sens.tldr: The paper develops two provably sample-efficient offline reinforcement-learning algorithms for entropic risk in linear Markov decision processes.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning large language models with optimizers such as SGD and Adam normally requires backpropagation, whose memory demands become challenging as models grow. This benchmark investigates zeroth-order optimization as a route to adaptation without backpropagation. The motivation is especially relevant when training must fit within limited memory, including on-device settings.

The study broadens the investigation beyond conventional zeroth-order SGD. It compares techniques across five language-model families, three levels of task complexity, and five fine-tuning schemes. This scope lets the authors examine how optimization choices interact with the task and adaptation setup, rather than treating memory-efficient fine-tuning as a single algorithmic choice.

The reported findings emphasize task alignment, the role of the forward gradient method, and the balance between algorithmic complexity and fine-tuning performance. The paper also introduces enhancements involving block-wise descent, hybrid training, and gradient sparsity. Its contribution is both a comparative assessment and a set of directions for improving zeroth-order methods. The findings present a promising path toward lower-memory fine-tuning, with performance tied to the choices made about training and optimization.
icml-2024-revisiting-zeroth-order-optimi.tldr: This benchmark studies a broad range of backpropagation-free fine-tuning methods and identifies optimization choices that matter for memory-efficient LLM adaptation.

paragraphs: Low-Rank Adaptation keeps pretrained model weights frozen and learns an additional low-rank matrix. This reduces the number of parameters that need updating, but the training dynamics still depend on the optimizer. The paper improves those dynamics by adding a small preconditioner to each gradient step, with dimensions determined by the LoRA rank.

For rank r, the preconditioner is an r-by-r matrix that adjusts the gradient update. The authors derive it from a new Riemannian metric for low-rank matrices and theoretically show that it stabilizes feature learning in an infinite-width neural-network setting. This gives a geometric justification for the update while making the scope of the theoretical result explicit.

Experiments with language models and text-to-image diffusion models show substantially better convergence and reliability for SGD and AdamW. Training also becomes more robust to choices such as the learning rate. The implementation requires only a small optimizer-code change and introduces very little storage or runtime overhead in the reported experiments. These results make the method a practical modification to LoRA training as well as a theoretically motivated one.
icml-2024-riemannian-preconditioned-lora.tldr: A small geometrically derived preconditioner improves LoRA optimization, with theoretical stabilization and empirical gains in convergence and hyperparameter robustness.

paragraphs: Reconstructing an articulated object from one monocular video requires inferring its shape, movement, and camera parameters from limited views. These estimates depend on one another, so an error in one can disrupt the others. S3O addresses this problem with a two-phase process that learns both visible geometry and an underlying skeleton.

The first phase learns a coarse parametric model. The second develops motion and adds detail. Separating these stages reduces the complexity associated with estimating everything simultaneously. The method also avoids additional human annotations such as predefined parametric models, camera poses, and keypoints, removing prerequisites that can restrict the applicability of reconstruction methods.

The authors introduce the PlanetZoo dataset and evaluate S3O on it alongside standard benchmarks. They report more accurate 3D reconstructions, plausible skeletons, and approximately 60% less training time than the state-of-the-art comparison. These findings support staged optimization as a way to improve both efficiency and robustness when viewpoints are limited. The skeleton result concerns plausibility, while the geometric reconstruction result concerns improved accuracy in the reported evaluations.
icml-2024-s3o-a-dual-phase-approach-for-.tldr: S3O reconstructs articulated shape and skeleton in two phases, improving reported accuracy and cutting training time by approximately 60%.

paragraphs: Predicting the mean-field Hamiltonian matrix is one way to use machine learning for molecular problems within density functional theory. A major obstacle is obtaining enough labeled training examples. This paper identifies a self-consistency principle in Hamiltonian prediction and uses it to train models without requiring labeled data.

The proposed self-consistency training is described as an exact training method. Its significance is that the task’s own consistency requirement can supply a training basis, allowing the model to use large amounts of unlabeled data. It also changes how computational effort is spent: instead of running DFT to generate a separate collection of supervised labels, the method amortizes DFT calculation across a set of queries.

Experiments show improved generalization when labeled data are scarce and when evaluation data differ from the training distribution. They also show greater efficiency than generating labels through DFT. Together, these findings support self-consistency as both a source of training information and a way to spread computation across predictions. The resulting benefit is broader applicability of Hamiltonian prediction at larger scales.
icml-2024-self-consistency-training-for-.tldr: Self-consistency training learns DFT Hamiltonian predictions without labels, improving reported generalization and efficiency relative to DFT label generation.

paragraphs: In a multi-agent system, agents may need to coordinate actions taken at different times. The paper represents this asynchronous coordination through a Stackelberg game, which supplies a hierarchical decision structure. It argues that existing reinforcement-learning approaches built around this structure face scalability restrictions arising from their network architectures or environmental settings.

The proposed Stackelberg Decision Transformer, called STEER, combines three elements: the game’s hierarchy, autoregressive sequence modeling, and exploratory multi-agent reinforcement learning. Sequence modeling provides a way to represent decisions in order, while the hierarchy organizes how those decisions relate. The reinforcement-learning component brings exploration into the process of learning coordinated behavior.

The authors report applicability across varied task types and environmental configurations. In complex experimental scenarios, STEER outperforms strong baselines and shows convergence toward Stackelberg equilibrium strategies. That convergence is an experimental finding in the supplied account. The broader contribution is an architecture that brings ordered decision modeling and hierarchical game structure together to handle asynchronous coordination, addressing the scalability problems that motivate the work.
icml-2024-sequential-asynchronous-action.tldr: STEER combines Stackelberg game structure, autoregressive modeling, and reinforcement learning to improve asynchronous coordination among agents.

paragraphs: Image registration aligns two views of the same content, including views captured by different sensors or with substantial appearance changes. Sparse feature matching is efficient but can struggle where there is little texture. Dense alignment offers greater accuracy but needs a good initial alignment. This paper combines the two approaches into a sequential procedure.

Its Sparse-to-Dense Multimodal feature Extractor, SDME, uses a multi-task network to predict features for both sparse matching and dense alignment. Registration begins with sparse matching to establish an initial solution. Dense alignment then refines that solution. The first stage therefore supplies the initialization needed by the second, while the shared feature extractor supports both operations.

Experiments on MSCOCO, GoogleEarth, VIS-NIR, and VIS-IR-drone demonstrate strong performance on multimodal cases. The authors also report that models trained initially on single-modal datasets can be fine-tuned using smaller multimodal datasets. This supports the approach’s generalization across imaging conditions. Its practical value comes from joining efficient initial matching with detailed refinement and supporting adaptation when multimodal training data are comparatively limited.
icml-2024-sparse-to-dense-multimodal-ima.tldr: SDME learns features for sparse matching and dense refinement together to align images across sensors and appearance changes.

paragraphs: Pruning removes parts of a neural network to compress it, but successful compression does not establish that a method has found the sparsest effective network. This paper investigates that distinction using a synthetic dataset called Cubist Spiral. The authors carry out 485,838 experiments with a range of state-of-the-art pruning algorithms.

A new combinatorial search algorithm identifies ideal sparse networks for comparison. Against those reference networks, the tested pruning methods show a substantial performance gap. The authors attribute the gap to poor behavior under overparameterization, disconnected paths created within networks, and optimization that becomes stuck in inferior solutions. Problems persist even when methods receive the optimal width and initialization.

These findings are striking within the study because the networks and dataset are simple. They show that finding a compact result through pruning can remain far from recovering an ideal sparse structure, even in comparatively controlled conditions. The evidence concerns the algorithms and synthetic setting examined, and motivates further work on pruning methods that more reliably approach true network sparsity.
icml-2024-sparsest-models-elude-pruning-.tldr: A large synthetic study finds that current pruning methods fall well short of ideal sparse networks, even with favorable initialization and width.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes difficult when an environment changes over time. The paper proposes that such non-stationarity can propagate through causal relationships during state transitions, accumulating into more complicated changes. From this perspective, modeling every observed change explicitly may miss an opportunity to work with a more stable representation of where the changes originate.

The Causal-Origin REPresentation algorithm, or COREP, uses a guided updating mechanism to learn a stable graph representation of the state. The representation is intended to implicitly trace the causal origin of non-stationarity. Policy learning then uses this representation, with the aim of maintaining useful behavior despite changes in the environment.

The authors provide theoretical analysis grounded in their causal interpretation and report experimental performance above existing methods on the non-stationarity problems evaluated. These findings support the use of causal-origin representations for resilient policy learning. The contribution combines a proposed explanation of how environmental change becomes complex with an algorithm that acts on that explanation, shifting attention toward learning a stable state representation.
icml-2024-tackling-non-stationarity-in-r.tldr: COREP learns a stable graph representation intended to trace the causal origins of environmental change and improve reinforcement-learning resilience.

paragraphs: Multivariate time-series analysis includes forecasting future values, filling gaps, and identifying anomalies. UP2ME aims to support these tasks through one pretraining framework even before the downstream task is specified. It separates learning temporal patterns within individual channels from learning dependencies between channels, addressing these relationships at different stages.

Pretraining uses single-channel sequences of varied lengths in a masked autoencoder and deliberately excludes cross-channel dependencies. Once a task and its settings are known, the framework expresses the task as a particular mask-reconstruction problem. This lets the frozen pretrained model produce sensible solutions before task-specific fine-tuning. Multivariate fine-tuning then uses the pretrained encoder to construct a graph of channel dependencies.

Experiments on eight real-world datasets show state-of-the-art performance in forecasting and imputation, with anomaly detection approaching the performance of task-specific methods. The distinction among these outcomes matters: the strongest reported comparative results concern forecasting and imputation. Overall, the framework demonstrates a route from reusable single-channel pretraining to task-specific, cross-channel adaptation, while retaining useful behavior before any fine-tuning.
icml-2024-up2me-univariate-pre-training-.tldr: UP2ME learns reusable single-channel time-series representations, then adds cross-channel structure to support forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection.

paragraphs: Scaling a model is most useful when additional computation produces dependable improvements in quality. The paper argues that recommendation architectures have lacked this behavior because their mechanisms for growing models are inefficient. Wukong combines a new architecture with a matching upscaling strategy to investigate more effective scaling for recommendation.

The architecture consists entirely of stacked factorization machines. Its design allows increasing depth and width to capture diverse interactions of arbitrary order. This matters because enlarging the network also expands the interactions it can represent. The architecture and scaling strategy are therefore designed together, linking model growth to the relationships the recommendation system can learn.

On six public datasets, Wukong consistently exceeds the quality of the state-of-the-art models evaluated. On an internal large-scale dataset, it retains that advantage and exhibits a scaling law across two orders of magnitude in model complexity, extending beyond 100 GFLOP per example. These results provide empirical evidence for useful recommendation-model scaling over the tested range, including a region where the compared approaches fall short.
icml-2024-wukong-towards-a-scaling-law-f.tldr: Wukong combines stacked factorization machines with coordinated scaling to improve recommendation quality across a broad tested range of model complexity.
